newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Rebel Dnestr region defies Moldova in Sunday poll.
newsitem.headline: Rebel Dnestr region defies Moldova in Sunday poll.

text.p: Moldova's rebel Dnestr region holds its own presidential election on Sunday, in defiance of the rest of the country which chose a new president on December 1 and calls Dnestr's poll illegitimate.

Dnestr's two presidential hopefuls are current leader Igor Smirnov, 55, elected local president in 1991 and backed by Russian ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky, and Vladimir Malakhov, 44, a less well-known local company manager.
"I want the election to take place and Smirnov to win the majority of votes. His position has been firm, and your republic exists," Zhirinovsky said in a appeal on Dnestr television.
Smirnov, a tall, balding Soviet-era industrial manager, used to run one of the biggest factories in the depressed industrial region. He is viewed as the sure winner of the poll.

Dnestr, a region of 700,000 people along Moldova's eastern border with Ukraine, broke away in 1990 on fears its mostly Slav residents could be sidelined if Moldova merged with ethnic kin in next-door Romania.
Hundreds were killed in a bloody war between Moldovan security forces and Dnestr separatists in 1992 and the bloodshed was only stopped by the intervention of Russian troops.

Moldovan talks with Dnestr over its future status, mediated by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, Russia and Ukraine, are stalemated over separatist demands for full independence. Moldova offers broad autonomy.
"The course towards strengthening the statehood of the Dnestr republic and its international recognition will be continued," Smirnov's election manifesto says.
Malakhov has the same separatist rhetoric: "I think we should be firm to safeguard the independence of our state."
But Moldova remains adamant on the issue of its integrity.

"These elections will have no political or legal effect," president-elect Petru Lucinschi said in a statement. "I have assumed responsibility as president of all Moldovan citizens, including people of the eastern region."

Lucinschi, who defeated the incumbent Mircea Snegur in Moldova's December 1 presidential election run-off, boasts of good ties in Moscow and promises to use them to influence Dnestr leaders to help resolve the conflict.
The head of the OSCE mission in Moldova also backed Moldovan territorial integrity.

"Elections in Transdnestr...cannot change the fact that there is one subject of international law and that the countries of the OSCE support -- and will continue to support -- the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Moldova," Donald Johnson said in a statement.
Dnestr faces economic hardships stemming from the lack of reforms -- rapid elsewhere in Moldova -- and local residents are nostalgic for the "stable" times of the former Soviet Union.
Russia is heavily involved in the region, which it won from the Turks in the 18th century, and has 6,000 troops there. Smirnov said the troops should stay.
"I will fulfil the will of the Dnestr people and ensure that the contingent of Russian troops stays in the region as a guarantor of its security and stability," his manifesto said.
Communists and nationalists, who make up the majority in the Russian State Duma and back Dnestr's claims for full independence, have appealed to local residents to choose Smirnov on Sunday.
